messages.content:
Subject: Various
Hi team — a few things. First, the rota for February is attached; please check your shifts and flag clashes by Friday. Second, we need a decision on the training budget — $3,200 for the two courses, ideally approved this week so we can book places. Third, the office kitchen fridge will be cleaned out on Monday; anything unlabelled will be thrown away. Thanks all!

Your colleague is right, and the single reply you got is the predictable result: a multi-ask email gets answered at the level of its easiest ask. Whoever replied dealt with the fridge or the rota — the item that cost them least — and the budget decision, the only one that needed thought, is still pending, now buried in a thread titled "Various" that nobody will reopen.

The split, with each email carrying one ask, one owner group, and a subject that does its job:

**Email 1 — to all staff.** Subject: "Action by Fri Jan 29: check your February rota shifts". Body: the rota, the clash deadline, where to flag problems. One ask, one date.

**Email 2 — to the budget approver only.** Subject: "Decision needed this week: $3,200 training budget for two courses". Body: the courses, the cost, why this week (places are held until bookings confirm), and the default if unapproved — the places are released. Notice this email should never have gone to the whole team: most recipients could not act on it, and every recipient who cannot act on an ask learns to treat your asks as scenery.

**Email 3 — to all staff, sent Monday morning.** Subject: "Fridge clean-out Monday Feb 1: unlabelled food will be thrown away". Sent when it is timely, not bundled into last week's traffic.

The underlying rule: an email is a unit of action. One email, one ask, one audience that can perform it. Bundling feels efficient for the sender and is expensive for everyone else — each bundled item competes with the others for the reader's single reply, and the item that loses is usually the important one, because important asks take thought and the fridge does not. Unbundle, and each ask gets its own thread, its own subject, and its own chance.

There is an email thread in my team with 23 replies about the office move. It has forked into arguments about parking, desks, and the lease date, and new people keep getting added. It needs to die. How?

You kill it with a summary-and-restart: one final email that closes the thread by absorbing it, then starts fresh threads for anything still alive. The technique works because long threads die of their own weight — nobody can find the current state inside 23 replies — so the killer email's real job is to become the new, single source of truth.

Composed shape, sent as a reply to the thread so it inherits the audience:

"Closing this thread — it now covers three separate topics and the decisions are getting lost. Summary of where things stand, which supersedes everything above:

**Decided.** Move date is Saturday, February 20, 2027 (confirmed with the landlord, Tuesday). Desk plan v2 is final — link below.
**Still open, now in their own threads.** (1) Parking allocation — owner: Sam; new thread started today, decision needed by Friday, January 29, 2027. (2) The old-office lease exit — owner: Ines; she will open a thread when the landlord replies.
**Dropped.** The hot-desking debate: the desk plan settles it; if you disagree, take it to the Friday team meeting, not to email.

Please do not reply to this thread further — replies go to the new threads, so each topic has one home."

Three mechanics matter. It replies to the thread rather than starting fresh, because the audience must encounter the closure in the place they are watching. It declares itself the superseding summary — "which supersedes everything above" — giving future readers permission to read one email instead of twenty-four. And it does not just kill; it re-homes the living topics with owners, because a thread killed without re-homing resurrects within the week, usually with "as I said in the other thread…" at the top.

Expect one or two replies anyway, from people who read the last message first. Answer those with a link to the new thread and nothing else. Threads die the way they lived: by example.
Half my team seems to cc everyone on everything "for visibility". The other half complains they cannot find the emails that actually need them. Is there a rule for cc that I can just announce?

Yes, and it fits in one sentence you can announce verbatim: **To means you act; Cc means you watch — and the first line of the email says who is who.** Most cc chaos is not malice; it is ambiguity. Recipients cannot tell whether they were sent the email to do something, to know something, or because the sender was covering themselves — so they either act on everything (duplication) or file everything (your second problem).

The first-line convention does the sorting at the source. Every email with more than one recipient opens: "Action: Marta (approve the rota). For information: the rest of the team." Twelve words, and eleven people can file the email with a clear conscience while one person knows the task is theirs. The cc list becomes what it should be — a subscription to awareness — instead of a fog of implied responsibility.

Two supporting rules make the announcement stick. First, a cc is a promise by the sender: "I judge this worth your awareness." Cc'ing a director "for visibility" on a routine thread is spending their attention to buy your safety, and teams that normalise it find directors filtering the whole team's mail. Cc up sparingly, and when you do, say why in that first line: "Cc: Priya, because this changes the February numbers she reports." Second, nobody may treat a cc as an assignment — if you want someone to act, they go in To and get named in line one. That rule protects receivers from the worst pattern in office email: the task that was "assigned" by cc, discovered three weeks later by a sender asking why it is not done.

Announce it, model it in your own mail for a month, and gently return violations with the first line rewritten. The team's inbox volume will not drop much. The signal inside it will transform.
Read fixtures/thread-wrong-question.txt. This thread went in circles for a week. I have a suspicion about why but I want your read.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
From: Dana (Finance) — Monday, January 11, 2027
Subject: Monthly pack
Quick question: which budget code should the agency invoices go under — the old one (4400) or the new structure's code? The pack closes Friday and I cannot finish without it.

From: Lee — Monday, January 11, 2027
The pack timeline is tight this month; we are aiming to close by Thursday if possible.

From: Marta — Tuesday, January 12, 2027
Agree the timeline matters. Last month we closed on the Friday and it was fine.

From: Lee — Wednesday, January 13, 2027
Update: the timeline slipped; we are now closing next Monday.

Your suspicion is almost certainly this: the thread circled for a week because nobody answered the question that was asked. Dana asked a specific, answerable question — which budget code, 4400 or the new one — with a deadline attached. Three replies followed, all fluent, all responsive-sounding, and all answering a different question: the pack's timeline. The thread has the shape of conversation and the content of three monologues passing in the night.

It happens for recognisable reasons. The timeline was the topic the repliers had opinions about; the budget code required knowledge or a lookup. Replying about the timeline feels like participating while costing nothing. And each reply raised the social price of returning to Dana's question, because by Wednesday, answering it means visibly noticing that two colleagues did not.

The repair, which any participant can still perform, is to name the miss without blame and answer the actual question: "Re-reading Dana's original: the open question is the budget code, and the pack is waiting on it. Answer: the new structure's code — 4400 closed with the old structure in December; finance confirmed this in the migration note. Dana, shout if you need the mapping table." Two sentences of substance, one of framing, zero reproach — naming the miss factually ("the open question is…") lets everyone save face while the thread snaps back to its purpose.

The habit to build, for yourself first: before replying to any thread, re-read the original message and state its question in your head. If your reply does not address that question, either answer it, say plainly "I cannot answer the code question — that is Ines's — but on the timeline…", or do not reply. A reply that declares its own scope is a contribution. A reply that silently changes the subject is how a one-day question takes a week.

When should I reply-all and when should I take a conversation private? I seem to get it wrong in both directions — group threads I should have narrowed, and private replies that left the group uninformed.

The test is one question: who else needs this information to do their job, and who is merely interested? Reply-all serves the first group. Taking it private serves everyone's attention. Get the classification right and the mechanics follow.

**Reply-all when your answer changes the state for the group.** The decision, the correction, the new date, the "that was my error, the right figure is X" — anything the whole list is working from. The classic failure here is the private correction: you spot the wrong figure, tell the sender one-to-one, and eleven people keep working from the wrong number for a week. Corrections, decisions, and schedule changes are public goods; privatising them is a false courtesy.

**Take it private when the thread narrows to a subset.** The moment a twelve-person thread becomes two people negotiating a detail — a meeting time, a drafting point, one client's specifics — the other ten are hostages. Move it, and say so in the group thread in one line: "Taking the scheduling detail offline with Sam; will post the outcome here." That sentence is the courtesy that makes narrowing legitimate: the group knows the topic is alive and where its answer will land.

**Take it private, always, for people matters.** Feedback, disagreement with a person's work, anything about an individual's circumstances — never in the group thread, even if the thread started there. The sender who raises it publicly may not have noticed the audience; your private reply both protects the subject and quietly teaches the norm.

And the meta-rule that fixes your "wrong in both directions" problem: when in doubt, ask which error is cheaper. An unnecessary reply-all costs ten people four seconds of triage. An unshared correction can cost a week of wrong work. So the bias, when genuinely unsure, is toward the group for facts — and toward private for everything about people. Facts are cheap to over-share and expensive to under-share; judgements of people are the reverse.
I want ammunition for our email-hygiene discussion: a thread with 40 people on it, 6 replies that everyone reads, average read time 4 minutes a reply. What does that thread cost in reading time?
Let us price it precisely, because vague claims about email cost convince nobody.

That one thread costs 960 person-minutes of reading — 16.0 person-hours. Two full working days, spent by forty people reading six replies. And that is the conservative figure: it counts only reading, at a brisk four minutes a reply, and excludes the original message, the re-reading when a later reply contradicts an earlier one, and the context-switch cost of returning to real work six times — the cost researchers consider the largest and your colleagues will feel in their bones even if you never cite it.

Use the number the right way in the discussion. The point is not "email is bad" — the thread may genuinely have been worth 16 hours, if it carried a decision forty people needed. The point is the exchange rate: every reply-all should be priced before it is sent, in the sender's head, as "this costs the group 40 × 4 = 160 minutes — is what I am adding worth 2.7 hours of the company's attention?" Replies that survive that question are welcome at any length. Replies that do not — the "thanks!", the "agreed" with no addition, the question only one recipient can answer — are revealed as what they are: small expenses charged to forty other people's days.

One more figure for your slide, if you want it: a single habitual reply-all sender, ten such threads a month, is spending the group roughly 160 person-hours a month — a full-time colleague's entire month, consumed four minutes at a time. Hygiene discussions fail on exhortation and succeed on arithmetic. You now have the arithmetic.

I need to email someone senior in another division who I have never met, to ask for twenty minutes of their expertise on a supplier problem. I do not want to sound presumptuous or desperate. How do I write it?

A cold ask inside a company succeeds on three signals: you have done your homework, the ask is small and specific, and saying no costs the reader nothing socially. Most failed cold asks miss the second — they ask for "a chat sometime about the supplier landscape", which is an unbounded commitment from a stranger, and gets the answer unbounded requests deserve.

Composed shape:

"Subject: Twenty minutes on the Harrow Print dispute — your name came from June Okafor

Hello — June suggested I write to you; she said you handled the print-supplier consolidation in 2024 and that our current dispute rhymes with it.

The specific question: our supplier is claiming the volume rebate does not apply because our orders were split across two accounts. Before I respond, I want to understand whether that argument has been run before and how it ended. I have read the contract clause and the account history — this is the one point I cannot settle from documents.

Would twenty minutes suit you, any time in the week of Monday, February 8, 2027? I will come to your office or take a call, whichever is easier, and I will bring the two contract pages so no preparation is needed from you. If this is a bad month, no reply needed — I will take silence as a no with no hard feelings, and June has a second name for me."

Count the signals. The referral is named in the subject, which converts a stranger's email into a colleague's errand. The homework is visible — one specific question, documents already read — which tells the reader their twenty minutes will be spent on judgement, not on educating you. The ask is bounded in time, place-flexible, and preparation-free. And the exit is graceful and pre-forgiven: "no reply needed" is not a trick, it is a genuine release, and paradoxically it raises response rates, because readers who are not cornered do not need to escape.

One thing to leave out: flattery about their brilliance. Senior people discount it instantly, and it frames the exchange as extraction. Respect is shown by preparation and brevity, not by adjectives.
Read fixtures/email-buried-ask.txt — it is my draft to my manager. She replied "fine" and I later learned she had not seen the actual request in it. Show me the fix.

messages.content:
Subject: Update on the training programme
Hi — quick update on the training programme. The two courses are now shortlisted and the team is enthusiastic. The provider has confirmed the syllabus covers everything we need, and the dates in March work for everyone. A couple of the team asked about the follow-up coaching day, which the provider can also run. The venue is available on the dates we discussed. All in all it is shaping up well. One thing: the total comes to $3,200, so I will need your approval on the budget before I confirm the booking. Let me know!

Your manager's "fine" was an honest reply to the email she thought she had read — a pleasant progress update — because the email is built like one: six sentences of good news with the request smuggled into sentence seven, phrased as an aside ("One thing:"). She approved the update. The $3,200 never stood a chance of being seen as a decision, because nothing in the document marks it as one — not the subject, not the position, not the typography of the ask.

The fix is reordering and honesty of labelling, using your own material:

"Subject: Approval needed by Fri Jan 29: $3,200 for the two training courses

Ask first: I need your approval for $3,200 to confirm the two training courses. The provider is holding the March dates until Friday, January 29, 2027; after that the booking and the price are not guaranteed. If I have not heard by Friday, I will release the dates rather than commit us — no chase needed.

The update behind it: both courses are shortlisted, the syllabus covers what we need, the team is enthusiastic, and the venue is available on the dates discussed. The provider can also run the follow-up coaching day the team asked about — that is a separate quote and not part of this approval."

Three repairs. The subject carries the ask, the amount, and the date — she can now triage it from her inbox as a decision. The ask sits in the first lines with its deadline and its default, so a reply of "fine" now unambiguously means "approved" (and note the default protects her too: silence releases the dates rather than committing her budget). And the update is still there, in its proper place — as context under the ask, where updates belong.

The general rule this teaches: in any email that contains a request, the request goes first and everything else is demoted to supporting material. Writers bury asks because leading with them feels blunt. It is not blunt; it is the difference between an email that works and one that gets a "fine".
I forward a lot of threads to my team with just "FYI" on top. They have started ignoring them. What should a forward actually include?

"FYI" is the least informative string in office life: it does not say why this thread, why now, why them, or what — if anything — you want done with it. Your team ignores your forwards because experience has taught them that opening one costs five minutes of archaeology to discover whether it mattered, and it usually did not. A forward earns its open with a two-line header, written by you, that does the archaeology for them.

The two lines answer: what this is, and what it means for the reader. Composed example:

"Forwarding the vendor's reply on the rebate dispute. **What matters for us: they have conceded the split-account point (message 3), so our February claim stands. No action needed — but if the vendor calls you directly, do not re-open the volume question; it is settled.** Thread below for the record."

Compare the work each version assigns. "FYI" assigns the reader the whole thread: find the relevant message among nine, identify the decision inside it, work out its bearing on their job. The header version assigns them fifteen seconds: the fact, its location if they want the evidence, the action boundary (none needed — but a live instruction about the vendor call, which is the one thing in the thread that could actually bite them). That last element is the one most forwards miss entirely: the "so what" is rarely the thread's content; it is the instruction the content implies for this specific reader.

Two habits complete the repair. Forward less: a forward should pass the test "this changes something my team knows or does", and most FYI traffic fails it — the sender was really saying "I have seen this, so I am covered", which is a filing action, not a communication. And when you do forward, forward once, with the header, rather than forwarding the same thread again as it grows; a team that receives the third instalment of a thread they never opened will open none of them. Your forwards are being ignored because they have been, on average, not worth opening. Make the average true, and the channel recovers faster than you would expect.
I am writing a runbook entry for restarting our search indexer when it wedges. The person using it will be on call, possibly at 3 a.m. What makes a runbook entry work at 3 a.m.?

A runbook is not documentation; it is a script for a tired person under pressure, and it should be written like one — imperative steps, one action each, with a verification line after every step that can do damage. At 3 a.m. your reader has no judgement to spare, so the runbook must lend them yours.

Composed entry, in the shape to copy:

**Restart the search indexer (wedged state)**
*Symptoms: search returns results older than 15 minutes; the indexer log shows no "batch complete" line for over 20 minutes.*

1. Check the indexer status page. **Verify:** it shows the job as RUNNING with no progress. If it shows FAILED, stop — use entry 7 instead; this entry is only for a wedged, still-running job.
2. Note the last completed batch number from the log. You will need it at step 5.
3. Stop the indexer service. **Verify:** the status page shows STOPPED within 60 seconds. If it still shows RUNNING after 2 minutes, do not force-kill — call the platform lead (number in the on-call sheet). A wedged indexer that resists a clean stop is a different problem.
4. Start the indexer service. **Verify:** the log shows "resuming from batch N" where N is the number you noted, or N+1.
5. Run the smoke query on the status page. **Verify:** results are current within 2 minutes. If search is still stale after 10 minutes, escalate — do not restart a second time.

Notice the load-bearing features. Each verify line tells the reader what correct looks like, so they are never guessing whether the step worked. The dangerous branches are pre-decided — the force-kill that a tired person would improvise is explicitly forbidden, with the alternative named. And the entry knows its own boundary: it states when to stop following it (second restart, FAILED state) and what to do instead. A runbook that cannot say "stop, this is no longer your problem" will eventually be followed off a cliff by someone too tired to argue with it.

Write every entry for the worst reader on the worst night, and the day shift will find it perfectly usable too.
Read our runbook draft in fixtures/runbook-cache-draft.txt and tell me if you would trust it at 3 a.m.

messages.content:
RUNBOOK — Clear the application cache
If the site is slow, the cache may need clearing. Log into the admin server and restart the cache service, then clear the cache from the admin panel. The site should speed up afterwards. If it is still slow, the problem is probably something else, maybe the database.

I would not trust it at 3 a.m., and I would barely trust it at 3 p.m. Read it as the on-call person: "if the site is slow" — how slow, measured where, and how do I know the cache is the suspect rather than the database the draft itself mentions at the end? "Restart the cache service" — which server, which service name, and what does success look like? "The site should speed up afterwards" — in how long, and by what measure? Every sentence requires a judgement the draft was supposed to supply, and it supplies none. Its most dangerous line is the last: having followed the entry and failed, the reader is waved at "maybe the database" with no next step, no escalation, and no warning about what not to try.

The rewrite, same procedure, runbook-grade:

**Clear the application cache**
*Use when: page loads exceed 4 seconds on the status dashboard AND the cache hit rate shows below 60%. If loads are slow but hit rate is normal, stop — this is not a cache problem; see the database entry.*

1. On the admin server, restart the service named app-cache. **Verify:** the service status shows running and the hit rate begins climbing within 2 minutes.
2. In the admin panel, choose Clear Cache and confirm. **Verify:** the panel shows "cache cleared" with a timestamp. Note the time — support will ask.
3. Watch the dashboard for 5 minutes. **Verify:** page loads fall below 2 seconds. If they do not, do not clear the cache a second time. Escalate to the platform lead and write the times in the incident channel.

The differences are the whole discipline: entry conditions that can be checked, named objects instead of "the server", a verification after each action, a stop rule, and an escalation that is a step rather than a shrug. Your draft describes the procedure. A runbook must conduct it.
I need to build an FAQ page for our clinic patients. I have a pile of real questions from the front desk. How do I turn a pile of tickets and questions into an FAQ that is actually useful?

By grouping before you write, and by letting the pile — not your imagination — decide the questions. A useful FAQ is a mirror of what people actually ask, in the words they actually use. The failure mode is the FAQ written from the organisation's chair: questions nobody asks ("What is our care philosophy?") answered at length, while the question asked forty times a month ("Can I bring my appointment forward if I am early?") is nowhere.

The method has three passes over your pile. **First, count.** Tally the front-desk questions by topic for a month. You will find the distribution is never flat: a handful of questions — booking changes, parking, what to bring, results timing, payment — will account for most of the pile. Those are your FAQ, in that order. An FAQ sorted by frequency is usable; one sorted by the org chart is a brochure.

**Second, phrase the questions as patients phrase them.** "Can I change my appointment without a fee?" beats "What is the rescheduling policy?" as a heading, because the reader scans for their own words. Keep the organisation's vocabulary for the answers, where precision matters — and even there, translate once: "Please give 24 hours' notice (that is, by the same time the day before) so we can offer the slot to another patient."

**Third, answer with the action first.** Each answer opens with what the reader can do, then the conditions: "Yes — call or use the portal up to 24 hours before. Inside 24 hours, call us anyway; we will try, and there may be a fee." An answer that begins with policy and ends with the action will be skimmed past by exactly the anxious reader it exists for.

Then keep it alive: the front desk logs new questions monthly, anything asked five times earns an entry, and any answer the desk has to correct twice gets rewritten. An FAQ is not a document you finish. It is a pressure valve you maintain — every question it absorbs is a phone call your desk did not have to take, and every stale answer in it actively manufactures the calls it was built to prevent.
We keep a decision log but it is a mess — some entries are essays, some are one line, and half the decisions are missing. What is the entry format, and how do we keep it current?

The log fails for the reason most logs fail: the entry costs too much to write, so entries get written late, long, or never. Fix the cost first. An entry is five fields, completable in three minutes, and deliberately too small to hold an essay:

**Date** the decision took effect. **Decision** in one sentence, active voice. **Decider** by name. **Why** in one or two lines — the reason that carried it, not the whole debate. **Revisit if** — the tripwire, or "not applicable".

A composed entry: "2027-01-15 · We renew hosting monthly rather than annually. · Decided by: Priya. · Why: the annual discount (about $400 a quarter) is worth less than the flexibility while the platform migration is undecided. · Revisit if: the migration decision lands, or monthly pricing rises."

The "revisit if" field is the one that separates a log from an archive. Decisions do not expire on schedule; they expire on events, and the entry should say which event. When the migration decision lands, anyone scanning the log can find every decision that was waiting on it — that is a genuinely powerful capability, and it costs eleven words per entry.

Keeping it current is a ritual, not a virtue. Three habits: the entry is written in the meeting or the thread where the decision lands, by the decider, before the next agenda item — never "later", because later is where the missing half went. Once a month, fifteen minutes of pruning: mark superseded entries as superseded (never delete — a struck-through decision with its successor linked is history; a deleted one is a hole people will fall into), and chase any decision the month's meetings made that has no entry. And the log has one home, linked from wherever decisions are announced, so "check the log" is a complete instruction.

Resist the urge to backfill the missing half perfectly. Mark the log's start of reliable coverage — "entries before January 2027 are incomplete" — and go forward clean. A log that is honest about its own gaps is usable; a log backfilled from memory is fiction with dates.

Audit this wiki page header for me — fixtures/wiki-page-header.txt. It is our payments onboarding page. The team suspects it is stale. The page says it was reviewed on September 14, 2026, its review cadence is 90 days, and today is Monday, January 18, 2027. How overdue is the review?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
WIKI — Payments onboarding (internal)
Owner: (blank)
Last reviewed: September 14, 2026
Review cadence: every 90 days
Review due: December 13, 2026
Let me put the overdue figure on it first — from the December 13 due date to today, January 18.

The review is 36 days overdue — due December 13, 2026, and untouched since September. But the overdue review is only the second-worst problem in this header. The worst is the blank owner. A page with an owner goes stale by accident; a page with no owner goes stale by design, because review reminders, if they exist, are delivered to nobody, and "the team should probably update this" has the same effect in every organisation ever studied: nothing.

Consider what this page is: payments onboarding — the document a new starter follows to learn how money moves. Thirty-six days overdue might be harmless, or the payment provider might have changed its console in November and the page now teaches a procedure that fails at step three. The header cannot tell you, and that is the point of the audit: staleness is not a sin, invisible staleness is. This header, to its credit, shows its dates — many pages hide them, which is worse.

Three repairs, in order. Name an owner today — a person, not a team — and put their name where the blank is. Have that owner do the review this week and either update the page or stamp it "reviewed, still accurate" with the new date; both are valid outcomes, and the second is underused — a page confirmed current is worth more than a page silently assumed current. And shorten the loop: a 90-day cadence that slips 36 days is really a 126-day cadence; either resource the 90 or honestly set 120, because a cadence the organisation cannot keep teaches everyone that the dates on wiki pages are decorative — the exact belief that makes staleness invisible next time.
I made a template for project briefs and people still send me bad briefs — now badly formatted ones. What is wrong with my template approach?

A template that only names sections teaches layout, not thinking. Your team is filling in boxes — "Background:", "Options:", "Recommendation:" — and a box invites whatever text is nearest, which is why the briefs arrive badly formatted instead of badly thought: same content, better headings. A template that teaches carries prompts inside the sections — questions the writer must answer, in the order a reader needs them.

Compare the two versions of one section:

**Layout template.** "## Options" — and the writer pastes in three vendor descriptions of unequal length, one with costs, two without.

**Teaching template.** "## Options — for each: (1) what it is, in one line; (2) total cost over 36 months, money and staff time; (3) its worst real downside — if you support this option, write the downside its opponents would write; (4) what would have to be true for this to be the right choice. If an option has no honest downside, you have not understood it yet."

The prompt does three jobs a heading cannot. It sets the unit of comparison (36 months, both currencies of cost) so options arrive comparable instead of adjacent. It embeds the standard — the supporter-written downside — at the moment of writing, not in a style guide nobody opens. And it gives the writer a self-check: a section that cannot answer the prompts is visibly unfinished to its own author, which is where you want the quality control to live.

Apply the same treatment to the other sections: the situation prompt asks "what is true that nobody disputes?"; the recommendation prompt asks "complete this sentence: I recommend X because ___; my name is on it". Then add the template's final gift — an example. One filled-in brief, fictional and short, linked at the top. Writers imitate examples ten times more faithfully than instructions. Your template is not failing because your team cannot write. It is failing because it specifies where things go instead of what good looks like. Teach in the template, and the briefs will arrive pre-reviewed.
I am pruning our decision log. It has 47 entries; 11 are superseded by later decisions and 6 are duplicates of other entries. How many active entries should remain after pruning?
Straight arithmetic, but worth doing in the open because the pruned count becomes the figure you report.

Thirty active entries remain: 47 − 11 superseded − 6 duplicates = 30. Now the part that matters more than the count — how the 17 are removed. Superseded entries are not deleted; they are struck through in place, with a link to the decision that replaced them and the date of replacement. A future reader who lands on the old decision — from an old email, an old slide — needs the entry to exist precisely so it can redirect them; delete it and the old link leads nowhere, and the reader concludes the old decision stands. Duplicates are the exception: merge them into the surviving entry, note the merge, and delete the copy, because two live entries stating the same decision will eventually be edited separately and become a contradiction.

One audit worth doing while the log is open: of the 11 superseded, check how many were superseded by a decision that itself has an entry. In most logs, some replacements were never logged — the old decision was overturned in a meeting and only its ghost remains. Those are your missing entries, and the pruning session is the cheapest moment to write them: five fields, three minutes each, while the people who remember are in the room. Report the result as you computed it: "Log pruned Monday, January 18, 2027: 30 active entries, 11 superseded and linked to their successors, 6 duplicates merged." A log whose maintenance is itself on the record is a log readers keep trusting.
Runbook, wiki, or ticket — my team argues about where every piece of knowledge should live. Is there a clean rule?

There is a clean test, three questions in order, and it settles most of the arguments because the three homes are for three different kinds of knowledge.

**Will someone need this at 3 a.m., under pressure, with no time to think?** Then it is a runbook entry. Runbooks hold procedures for known situations: imperative steps, verifications, stop rules. The test is the hour and the stress, not the topic. A database failover is runbook material even if it happens twice a year, because when it happens, it happens at the worst moment and the reader's judgement is the scarcest resource in the room.

**Does it explain how something works, or why it is the way it is?** Then it is the wiki. Architecture, rationale, the history of a decision, how the billing model is structured — knowledge read in daylight, by someone building understanding. The wiki's reader has time and questions; the runbook's reader has neither. Material fails when it is filed by its subject instead of its reader: the failover explanation (wiki) and the failover procedure (runbook) are about the same system and must live in both places, cross-linked, written completely differently.

**Is it about one occurrence — this incident, this customer, this failure?** Then it is a ticket, and it stays a ticket. Tickets are the record of events: dated, owned, closed. The argument your team keeps having usually starts when an event record contains a general lesson — the incident ticket that discovered the cache wedges when the moon is full. The rule for that: the lesson gets promoted. Write the runbook entry or the wiki paragraph, link it from the ticket, and close the ticket. A lesson left inside a closed ticket is a lesson buried with the event.

So: procedures for the pressured, explanations for the curious, records for the specific. When a document is failing its readers, it is almost always a filing error by this test — a wiki essay being followed at 3 a.m., or a procedure rotting inside a ticket nobody will ever reopen. Argue about the reader and the moment, not the topic, and the arguments mostly dissolve.

Read fixtures/faq-draft-and-tickets.txt. We drafted an FAQ from what we thought patients ask. The same file has the front desk's actual question counts for last month. Grade the draft against reality.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
DRAFT FAQ (from our assumptions)
1. What is our clinic's philosophy of care?
2. Which insurance networks are we part of?
3. Can I see a particular clinician?
4. What should I expect at my first appointment?

ACTUAL QUESTIONS AT THE FRONT DESK, LAST MONTH (counted)
- Changing or cancelling an appointment: 14
- Parking and finding the clinic: 9
- What to bring / how to prepare: 9
- When will my results be ready: 5

The draft fails against reality in the most common way: it answers the questions the clinic wishes patients asked. Let me total the real demand first, so the rebuild is driven by the count rather than by taste.

Thirty-seven counted questions, and the single biggest topic — changing or cancelling an appointment, 14 of them, 37.8% of all demand — does not appear in your draft at all. Neither do parking (9), what to bring (9), or results timing (5). Meanwhile the draft leads with the clinic's philosophy of care, which the front desk recorded zero times. This is not a criticism of the drafters' intentions; it is what every assumption-built FAQ looks like. Organisations write the questions that flatter them. Desks count the questions that inconvenience them, and those are the ones an FAQ exists to absorb.

The rebuild writes itself from the count, in the count's order: (1) How do I change or cancel an appointment — with the notice period and the fee, in the patients' own phrasing. (2) Where do I park, and how do I find the clinic — with the landmark directions the desk actually gives. (3) What should I bring and how should I prepare. (4) When will my results be ready, and how will I hear. Your draft's questions are not banned — insurance networks genuinely matter, and "first appointment" overlaps with question 3 — but they take their place after the demand, in the order the demand dictates.

One structural habit finishes the job: the FAQ is re-counted quarterly, and the counts live in the document's footer ("Topics ranked by front-desk counts, January 2027"). That line does quiet work — it tells the next editor the ordering is evidence, not preference, and it tells them exactly how to re-derive it when the counts change. An FAQ ranked by reality stays ranked by reality only if the ranking method survives its first author.

Set: Monday, February 1, 2027, 14:00–15:00. An hour is the right size if the review is a checkpoint rather than a rewriting session, and the agenda fits on one hand. Runbooks first: each owner confirms their entries were either exercised since the last review — a real use is the best audit — or re-read against the current system; any entry whose system changed gets updated in the room or scheduled with a date. Decision log second: prune superseded entries, link them to their successors, and chase the quarter's decisions that never got entries — the meetings know what they were, and three minutes per entry is the whole cost.

Two rules keep the quarterly rhythm from decaying into an annual panic. The review's output is a short note — what was confirmed, what was updated, what is overdue and whose it is — filed where the documents live, so the maintenance itself has a record. And an entry that comes up "confirmed still accurate" counts as a success, not a non-event: the review exists to convert silent assumptions about currency into dated statements of it. The documents your organisation runs on do not stay true by themselves. This hour, four times a year, is the price of being able to trust them at 3 a.m. — which is when their truth is worth the most.
Read fixtures/update-two-pages.txt. This update has to become one page for the steering group. I do not want to just shrink the font. What goes, and in what order?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
UPDATE — Harbour billing migration, month 3 (two pages, condensed here to its structure)
Page 1: a four-paragraph history of the billing system since 2019 and why migration was chosen; a paragraph on the vendor selection process; current state: data migration 70% complete; two of five interfaces live.
Page 2: the test cycle found defects in the invoice-rounding interface (fix in progress, due Friday); the training plan for billing staff (three sessions in February); a risk that the parallel-run period may extend by two weeks, adding bridging cost; a request that the steering group approve the contingency of $12,000 for the possible extension; team news (two joiners).

Cut in this order, because the order is the method: history first, process second, colour last — and protect the decision material with your life.

**First cut: the history.** Four paragraphs on the billing system since 2019 and the vendor selection process. The steering group approved this migration; they do not need it re-sold to them monthly. It compresses to one sentence — "Month 3 of the billing migration approved in October" — and anything a new member needs goes to an appendix. This cut alone is most of your page.

**Second cut: the mergeable detail.** Training plan: three sessions in February is a line, not a paragraph ("Training: three sessions in February, all billing staff"). Team news: one line or none — two joiners belong in a team update, not a steering document, unless the steering group owns hiring.

**Protected: state, risk, ask.** What survives untouched, because it is the update's actual payload: data migration 70% complete; two of five interfaces live; the invoice-rounding defect with its fix due Friday; the parallel-run risk at two weeks; and the $12,000 contingency ask — which, notice, appears on page 2 of the original, after the history. In the one-page version it is the third thing the reader meets.

The rebuilt skeleton: headline (month 3, on plan except the rounding defect), state in three lines, risk in two, ask in two, training and team news in one line each at the foot. The discipline generalises beyond this document: when cutting any ops update, ask of each paragraph "does the reader decide, act, or watch differently because of this?" History fails that test for a steering audience — they were the deciders. It is almost always the biggest block and almost always the first to go, yet writers cut it last because it was the hardest to write. Cut by the reader's need, not by the writer's effort, and two pages become one without touching the font.
My editor keeps saying my operations writing is "full of decisions nobody made". She means the passive voice, I think. Can you show me what she is hunting for?

She is hunting for sentences where something important happened and the grammar has deleted the human who did it. In operations writing this is not a style flaw; it is missing information — because a decision with no decider cannot be questioned, supported, or revisited. Here are the usual suspects, caught and repaired:

**"It was decided that the launch would be delayed."** Decided by whom, on what evidence? → "June delayed the launch on Friday, after the second failed test cycle." Now a reader who disagrees knows whose reasoning to examine — and June, named, will make the next such call more carefully.

**"The invoice was sent to the wrong client."** This one matters most: errors need owners even more than decisions do, because the fix lives with the owner. → "I sent the invoice to the wrong client; I have reissued it and added a check to the run." Notice the repair also adds the remedy — an owned error usually arrives with one; an ownerless one just hangs there, smelling of cover-up.

**"Concerns were raised about the timeline."** By whom, and were they answered? → "Theo raised the timeline concern in Tuesday's review; the answer is in the decision log." The passive version makes dissent sound like weather — present, authorless, ignorable.

**"The report will be updated in due course."** → "Sam updates the report by Friday, January 29, 2027." "In due course" is the passive voice's cousin: a deadline with the date removed.

The audit method is one question, applied to every sentence that reports a decision, an error, or a commitment: *who?* If the sentence cannot answer, rewrite it until it can. Keep the passive where it belongs — for processes and physics ("the file is compressed at midnight", "the office was flooded") no human is being hidden. Your editor is not polishing your prose style. She is restoring the cast list to a document whose readers need to know who holds each thread — which, in operations, is most of what the document is for.
My status updates go to a mixed audience — engineers and clinic managers. The engineers' jargon keeps confusing the managers, but the engineers say the precise terms matter. How do I write for both?

With an inline glossary: use the precise term once, gloss it in the same breath, and then use the term freely. The engineers keep their precision; the managers get a translation at the exact moment of need, without a separate document, a footnote hunt, or the faint condescension of a "simple version".

Watch it work on the sentences that actually cause trouble:

**Before.** "The SLA breach was caused by connection pool exhaustion after the campaign send."
**After.** "We breached our response-time promise (the SLA) because the database ran out of simultaneous connections (the pool) when the campaign email brought everyone in at once."

**Before.** "Failover completed; the system is now running on the secondary with no data loss."
**After.** "The backup system (failover) has taken over completely, and no information was lost." — here the gloss can replace the term in the sentence, because "failover" adds no precision the managers need; keep the term in the engineers' own log instead.

The judgement call per term: if the word will recur in the document, gloss once and reuse — the reader learns the vocabulary and your future updates get shorter. If it appears once, translate it away entirely; a glossary entry for a word used once is clutter. And gloss with consequences, not definitions: "connection pool" defined as "a set of reusable database connections" teaches nothing; "ran out of simultaneous connections, so patients queued" teaches everything, because it says what the term did to people the managers care about.

One more habit for mixed audiences: numbers and times are universal — every figure in your update is already bilingual. The more of the update's weight the numbers carry, the less the jargon matters. A status that reads "09:15–10:05, 1,240 of 9,600 patients affected, cause: the connection limit (above)" communicates across the whole room. Precision is not the enemy of clarity here; unexplained precision is.
A paragraph in my draft update says: "Churn was 8.6% last quarter and 7.9% this quarter, which is an improvement." My editor says the paragraph is doing less than it should. What is missing?
What is missing is the arithmetic your editor can feel but the paragraph never performs: how big the improvement is, stated both ways. Let me run the two numbers your sentence owes the reader.

The improvement is 0.7 percentage points — and, in relative terms, an 8.1% fall in the churn rate itself (from 8.6 to 7.9 per hundred customers, the rate dropped by 8.1395…%, which rounds to 8.1%). The paragraph should carry both, because they answer different readers' questions:

"Churn fell to 7.9% from 8.6% last quarter — down 0.7 percentage points, an 8.1% relative improvement in the rate."

Percentage points are the honest unit for the change in a rate: they cannot be spun, and every reader interprets them the same way. The relative figure is the one that conveys significance — a 0.7-point fall on a rate of 30% would be minor; on a rate of 8.6% it is a real movement, and the 8.1% says so. Publishing only the points undersells a genuine improvement; publishing only the relative figure ("churn down 8%!") invites the reader to wonder what is being hidden, and in less honest documents it is the standard trick for making small movements look large — which is why your editor's instinct fired. The defence against suspicion is to print both, always, and let the reader choose their lens.

One more completion the paragraph owes: a cause or an honest absence of one. "…driven mainly by the onboarding change in November" or "…we do not yet know why; the analysis lands Friday, February 5, 2027." A movement without a cause invites the reader to invent one, and invented causes have a way of becoming next quarter's strategy. Your editor is right that the paragraph underperforms: two numbers and the word "improvement" is a claim. The same numbers with the change computed both ways and a cause attached is information.
A writing coach told me to read my status updates aloud before sending, and fix any sentence I stumble on. That sounds like superstition. Is there anything in it?

It is one of the most practical editing techniques there is, and the mechanism is not mysterious. Reading silently, your brain auto-corrects: it supplies missing words, repairs broken grammar, and skims over the clause you wrote twice. Reading aloud disables the auto-correct, because your mouth has to physically produce every word in order — and the sentence you stumble on is almost always a sentence with a structural fault your eyes had been papering over.

The stumbles have a small taxonomy worth knowing. **The breath stumble:** a sentence you cannot finish in one breath is carrying more than one thought, and a reader will lose its thread at the same place your lungs did. Split it. **The re-read stumble:** you go back to the start of a clause because the grammar misdirected you — a pronoun whose owner is ambiguous, a modifier attached to the wrong noun. Your readers will re-read it too, or worse, not re-read it and take away the wrong meaning. **The tongue stumble:** clustered jargon and consonant piles — "the sixth successive sync check" — which in operations writing usually marks a place where the writer was transcribing a system instead of explaining a state.

Try it on the kind of sentence that ships broken every week: "The migration, which was originally scheduled, before the vendor delay, for completion in the first week of February, has now been moved to the second week, pending confirmation." Aloud, you will stumble at the nested clauses — and the fix the stumble dictates is the pyramid in miniature: "The migration moves to the week of Monday, February 8, 2027 (was: first week of February). Cause: the vendor delay. Confirmation expected Wednesday." Nothing was added; the sentence was re-sequenced until a human voice could carry it, which is the same test as whether a tired reader can.

It costs ninety seconds for a page. Do it for anything that goes to more than five people, and for anything — at any length — where being misunderstood is expensive. Your eyes are the author's accomplice. Your ears are the reader's advocate. Edit with the advocate.
Read fixtures/update-numbers-in-prose.txt. My lead says the figures are "trapped in the prose". What does she mean and how do I free them?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
UPDATE — Fernhill Bakery Group, January
Revenue came in at $412,000, which compares with a plan of $460,000, while December's figure was $398,000. Deliveries rose to 18,400 from 17,900 in December. Waste was 4.1% against a target of 3.5%, and staff costs were 31% of revenue, within the 30–32% band. Two outlets opened, as planned, and none closed.

She means your reader has to mine the numbers out of the sentences — holding each figure in memory while hunting for the one it should be compared with, three clauses later. Fourteen numbers live in this paragraph; by the end, a normal reader retains perhaps three, and not necessarily the important ones. Figures in a grid do the comparing for the reader, because position carries the relationship. Freed, your update looks like this:

**January — Fernhill Bakery Group**

| Measure | Actual | Plan / target | Last month |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $412,000 | $460,000 | $398,000 |
| Deliveries | 18,400 | — | 17,900 |
| Waste | 4.1% | 3.5% | — |
| Staff costs | 31% of revenue | 30–32% band | — |
| Outlets opened | 2 | 2 | — |

One prose sentence survives above the table, and it is the one the table cannot say: "Revenue missed plan while deliveries grew — we delivered more and earned less per delivery, which is the month's real story."

Notice what the format change reveals. In prose, the revenue story (missed plan, up on December) and the deliveries story (grew) sat in separate sentences and never met; in the grid, the eye puts them side by side in a second. The empty cells are information too — waste has no last-month figure in your draft, which the table exposes as a visible gap instead of an invisible one. And scanning replaces reading: a director can now absorb the month in ten seconds and spend their attention on the one sentence that interprets it.

The rule is not "tables good, prose bad". Prose is for narrative, cause, and judgement — the things with verbs in them. Tables are for any set of numbers that share comparisons. Your paragraph tried to make prose do a grid's job, and the figures were trapped doing penance for it. Free them, and keep one sentence of prose for the meaning — that division of labour is most of operations editing in a single move.
I open most work emails with things like "As you know..." or "I wanted to reach out regarding..." A colleague calls this throat-clearing. What should the first line be instead?

The first line should be the point. Throat-clearing is everything a writer says to warm up before the message starts — and it taxes every reader for the writer's comfort. Worse, your three openers are not neutral filler; each quietly misfires. "As you know…" claims the reader knows something they may not, and reads as a small rebuke when they do not. "I wanted to reach out regarding…" announces the act of emailing instead of the content — the reader learns that a message exists, which the fact of the message already told them. "Just circling back" apologises for a follow-up that needed no apology and still does not say what it is following up.

The replacements are not blunter versions of the same warm-up; they are the message itself, promoted to the top:

**Instead of** "As you know, the rota has been under review, and I wanted to reach out regarding the outcome…" → "The weekend rota decision is made: one weekend in three, from Saturday, February 6, 2027. Details below."

**Instead of** "I am writing to let you know that the training dates have been confirmed and to ask whether…" → "Training dates confirmed for March — and I need your two nominees by Friday, January 29, 2027."

**Instead of** "Just circling back on the sandbox spend…" → "Second ask: $6,400 sandbox spend, needed by Wednesday, January 27, 2027. Default if unapproved: the migration pauses."

The test is deletion: read your first two sentences and ask whether the email loses information if they vanish. If not, they were throat-clearing, and the real first line is sentence three. There is one legitimate exception — an email delivering bad news to someone who will be hurt by it earns a sentence of human framing before the fact, because the reader is a person before they are a processor. But that framing should be chosen, brief, and about them ("This is the outcome you were hoping against, and I am sorry") — not a formula that delays every message you send, in every circumstance, forever.
I edit my team's drafts. When I rewrite heavily, people get defensive and the documents start sounding like me instead of them. How do I edit someone else's writing without stealing it?

By editing in two passes with different permissions — and by making your suggestions things the author can refuse. The defensiveness you are meeting is rarely about the edits themselves; it is about discovering, in a circulated document, that your judgement was replaced wholesale by someone else's. An author who finds their meaning intact and their sentences improved is grateful. An author who finds their voice gone feels demoted, and starts routing drafts around you — which costs you the chance to catch the real errors.

**Pass one: meaning only, as queries, not changes.** Read for the document's job: is the decision findable, the ask dated, the owner named, the numbers compared? Everything you find goes in the margin as a question the author answers in their own words — "Who decided this? The sentence needs a name", "This figure needs its plan beside it", "Is the deadline Friday the 22nd or the 29th?" Queries teach: the author fixes the fault and, fixing it, learns to see it. Rewrites conceal: the document improves and the author does not.

**Pass two: sentences, offered as options.** Only now touch the prose, and lightly — the throat-clearing opener, the passive decision, the paragraph that should be a table. Where you change a sentence, keep the author's vocabulary and rhythm where you can; where you cannot, present your version beside theirs rather than instead of it. An author who chooses between two wordings keeps ownership of both. Track-changes culture matters here: visible edits are an audit trail of respect; silent rewrites are a coup.

Two boundaries protect the relationship. Never edit a document's position — if you disagree with the recommendation, that is a conversation with the author, not a correction; an editor who reverses a conclusion by red pen has stopped editing and started deciding, and the author will experience it exactly that way. And say what is working, specifically, when it is: "your blocked section names an owner and a date — that is the standard" is not flattery, it is calibration, and it makes your queries land as craft rather than criticism.

The goal to hold in mind: after your edit, the author should be able to defend every sentence in the document as theirs — because the judgements are theirs, the voice is theirs, and your contribution was to make both clearer. An editor whose authors keep sending drafts early, voluntarily, is doing it right. That is the metric; watch it, not the redness of your pen.
My two-page update runs to about 1,840 words. A true one-pager is roughly 550 words. What fraction of my draft has to go? I want the number before I start cutting.
Let us compute the cut precisely, so you start with the scale of the job rather than a feeling about it.

You need to cut about 70.1% of the draft — 1,290 of its 1,840 words — keeping roughly 30%. That figure usually lands as bad news, so let me reframe it before you start: a 70% cut is not a massacre, it is the normal distance between a document that records everything its writer knows and a document that serves its reader. Most two-page updates contain a page of history, context, and process that the audience either already has or does not need for the decision in front of them.

Cut in the order that makes the number painless. History and background first — in most updates that is 35–40% of the words and nearly none of the decisions; it compresses to a sentence or moves to an appendix. Process narrative second — how the team arrived at the state matters less than the state; the journey paragraphs become lines. What never gets cut to reach the number: the headline, the current state with its comparisons, the risks with dates, and the ask. If you reach 550 words and those are intact, the cut was editing. If you reached it by trimming those, it was amputation, and the page count is the only thing that improved.

One practical trick: cut in two passes with a rest between them. The first pass, to about 900 words, is easy — it is all deletion of the clearly dead. The second pass, to 550, is where the craft is, because now every paragraph is defensible and you must choose among live material by the reader's need alone. Writers who try to do both passes at once stall at 1,200 words and declare the target impossible. The number says otherwise: 70% sounds brutal, but it is the standard ratio between knowing and telling — and telling is the job.

Capstone test. Here is a real style of document from my team: "UPDATE: The project is progressing. It has been noted that the vendor deliverable is somewhat delayed and discussions are ongoing. It is hoped a decision on the extension can be reached in due course, as costs may be impacted." Rewrite it properly and tell me every principle you used.

Here is the rewrite first, then the principles — because the original's deepest flaw is that it contains almost no facts, so the rewrite must also show where facts have to be supplied. Bracketed items are facts the writer must fetch; a rewrite cannot invent them, and pretending otherwise would be the one sin worse than the original's vagueness.

**Rewrite.** "Harbour migration: the vendor's interface deliverable is 10 days late (due Friday, January 15, 2027; now forecast Monday, January 25, 2027 — [confirm forecast with vendor]). Owner of the delay: the vendor's test team; our contact is [name]. Cost impact: each further week of delay adds about [£/$ figure] in bridging costs. **Decision needed from the steering group by Wednesday, January 27, 2027: approve a two-week extension with the cost cap in the appendix, or direct us to invoke the delay clause.** Default if undecided: we invoke the clause, because the cap expires first."

Now the principles, in the order the original violated them:

**1. State, not weather.** "The project is progressing" is unfalsifiable — it is true of every project that has not been cancelled, including failing ones. The rewrite opens with the project's name and its one material fact: a deliverable is late, by a measured amount.

**2. Every actor named.** "It has been noted" and "discussions are ongoing" delete the humans. The rewrite names who is late, who owns it on our side, and who must decide. A document whose sentences have no subjects cannot be acted on, because action is something people do.

**3. Quantify or confess.** "Somewhat delayed" and "costs may be impacted" are quantities with the numbers removed. The rewrite gives days and demands a figure — and where the figure is genuinely unknown, it says so in brackets rather than covering the hole with an adverb. That honesty is a principle in itself: mark the gaps; do not plaster them.

**4. The ask is a decision, with a deadline and a default.** "It is hoped a decision can be reached in due course" is the passive dodge in full ceremonial dress — hope is not a mechanism. The rewrite asks for a specific choice between two named options, by a date, with the consequence of silence pre-decided and stated.

**5. The headline carries the news.** A reader who reads only the first sentence of the rewrite knows more than a reader who studies the original for a minute.

Hold the original and the rewrite side by side and the summary writes itself: the original is 41 words containing zero checkable claims; the rewrite is longer and contains nothing else. That ratio — checkable claims per document — is the whole discipline of operations writing in one measure. Everything else is technique in its service.
